newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan PM, foes call India talks breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan PM, foes call India talks breakthrough.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif said on Monday that Pakistan's agreement with arch-foe India on an agenda for peace talks was a major breakthrough because it prmised an attempt to settle the future of the Himalayan region of Kashmir.

It was the first time India had recognised Kashmir as disputed, Sharif told reporters at parliament after four days of talks between top foreign ministry officials of the two countries ended with a joint statement.
"It is a major breakthrough in Indo-Pakistan relations," Sharif told reporters
He said his government would continue the dialogue with India in sincere hope of solving all disputes.
Iqbal Haider, information secretary for opposition leader Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party's, called Monday's accord "a positive move forward towards a settlement of the Kashmir problem".

But Amanullah Khan, Pakistan-based leader of the militant Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front, called the agreed agenda a "complete disappointment " because it failed to recognise the Kashmiri people as a party to the dispute or promise them the right to decide their own future.

India rules two-thirds of the Moslem majority region of Jammu and Kashmir while Pakistan controls the remaining third. Two of the three wars fought between them since their independence from Britain in 1947 have been over Kashmir.

Khan, whose group seeks to reunite the region into an independent state, said in a statement that for Kashmiris, Monday's joint statement was "far worse" than a 1972 Indo-Pakistan peace accord in which the two sides pledged to solve the issue through bilateral talks.
"In short, the joint statement was a complete disappointment to patriotic Kashmiris," he said.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan, speaking in parliament, called the Islamabad talks a success that had opened up an opportunity for promoting friendly and a harmonious relationship between the two countries.
"It is a very progressive step and our satisfaction is that for the first time the issue of Jammu and Kashmir has been put on the agenda for working groups along with other issues," he said.
"Now, step by step, we will go ahead to solve the much important and the long-standing Jammu and Kashmir problem."

The joint statement issued after the talks between the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministry secretaries, or top career diplomats, said the two sides had agreed to set up working groups to tackle all outstanding issues dividing them.
India and Pakistan, both seen as threshold nuclear powers, agreed to halt hostile propaganda and avoid provocative actions.
The put peace and security and confidence-building measures at the top of the agenda, with Jammu and Kashmir second.
They also undertook to discuss their confrontation on the Siachen glacier, terrorism, drug trafficking, economic and commercial co-operation, and other issues.
